rv.q: Although Clint Dyer’s stirring take on Ken Kesey’s 1962 novel boldly reframes the story, the text can’t support his ideas.
Message of freedom still holds power

On paper it’s a solid metaphor for systematic oppression, that chimes with the civil rights era in which the play was written. But Kesey’s essentially libertarian allegory for how the system crushes bright, interesting and rebellious individuals does not really translate that well into a parable of collective solidarity.
That said, when he returns to the soil ruthlessly grabbed by genocidal invaders, it’s hard not to cheer.
Is it a rallying call to individuality and the exercising of free will to speak up and challenge those in authority?
This is nit-picking: the acting is brilliant, not only in the lead role but throughout the cast.

cn.t: Dyer's bold reimagining with an African American cast adds timely resonance to Kesey's tale, anchored by Pierre's storming performance as McMurphy, though critics question whether the original text fully supports this ambitious reframing.
